item.title: The Role of A Therapy Dog in Private Practice
item.description:
Therapy

The Role of A Therapy Dog in Private Practice

How my dog Monty changes the feel of the therapy room, and why it matters.

Posted September 13, 2026

Key points
  • A therapy dog offers clients a low-pressure way to settle into the room before the session asks more of them.
  • Research links animal-assisted therapy with lower anxiety and greater engagement across settings
  • A dog's unconditional, in-the-moment presence models something clinicians can learn from.
  • Whether Monty's timing and affection reflects intuition or learned behavior, the effect on clients is real.

When people find out my dog Monty is a therapy dog who works alongside me each day, I usually respond with, “Yeah, he’s the reason why about half my clients keep coming back.”

People laugh at what they consider a joke. But on the rare days when Monty can’t make it to the office, my clients’ reactions tell me everything I need to know about his role in the therapeutic process.

“Where’s Monty?!”

I can't help but hear an unspoken: “What exactly do you think I’m paying you for?”

Who Is Monty?

Monty (short for Montezuma) is an old guy now. He’s ten and a half and has been coming to work with me for the past seven years. He was certified through a local therapy-dog nonprofit in San Diego and along with his work in my office, we’ve volunteered together at schools and community events throughout San Diego. The university where I teach has also graciously allowed him to join me in the classroom, where his popularity amongst my students profoundly exceeds mine.

Monty was born for the job. His wolfish appearance elicits a broad range of initial reactions, from awe to occasional hesitance. Though the hesitation never lasts. Northern Inuit dogs were bred for their wolf-like appearance as well as to be exceptionally friendly. Monty himself is warm, calm, and interested in people.

Monty in Yoho National Park. British Columbia, Canada
Source: Matt Bishop

Monty's Ability to "Read the Room"

Monty will greet clients by resting his chin on their lap, looking up at their face, and patiently wait to be pet. I am sure to let clients know he will give them about as much attention as they give him. If they keep petting him, he’ll stay nearby and will probably plop across their feet for the hour. If they offer only a quick hello, he understands the assignment and returns to one of his two preferred spots: the blanket at the far end of the sectional or the ugly dark patch he has gradually created (and I've given up on cleaning) on my otherwise white rug by the door.

For the occasional client who isn’t particularly fond of dogs, Monty is perfectly happy to nap without interruption. He knows how to respect a boundary, especially when the alternative is sleep.

What Research Says About Therapy Dogs

Research suggests that therapy dogs can have a meaningful impact in a wide range of settings. Their presence has been associated with reduced anxiety among patients receiving care in emergency departments, intensive care units, and pediatric settings (Kline et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2025; Kelker et al., 2025). In mental and behavioral health settings, dog-assisted therapy has also been linked with improvements in social behavior, engagement, and motivation among pediatric psychiatric patients and adults in substance-use treatment (Fornefeld et al., 2023; Mittly et al., 2024).

Graduating from Therapy Dog Prep School
Source: Matt Bishop

Still, writing about the impact Monty has by citing research data and numbers feels a bit dry and detached. Monty’s value in the therapy room can’t be reduced to merely a statistic.

He gives clients a reason to smile before they have said a word. He provides a gentler way into a room where difficult topics are often discussed. A conversation about his favorite spots in the area, his favorite place to be pet, or what he was like as a puppy gives clients a few minutes to arrive and settle in before therapy starts to ask a bit more of them.

There are some moments when his timing makes me wonder precisely what his job is.

Often when a client becomes tearful, Monty will get up from across the room and rest his chin on their knees. Though part of me would like to think that he possesses some extraordinary clinical intuition. It is also possible that he has simply learned that crying humans tend to pet dogs. Either way, the effect is real.

Why Therapy Dogs Help Make Therapy More Effective

Therapy asks people to do something really brave: walk into a room, sit across from another person, and have a conversation about the parts of their lives they are having a tough time with. Monty makes that room feel a little less clinical and a little more human. He doesn't see people as a diagnosis and he doesn't see them as a project. Progress or no progress, he's excited to see them. He doesn't keep score on the hard sessions, and he doesn't need them to be any different than who they are today. He just wants to be present and with them in the here and now.

In all those ways and more, I want to be more like him.

Monty In His Spot On The Sectional
Source: Matt Bishop

item.title: The Evolution of Marriage Vows
item.description:
Marriage

The Evolution of Marriage Vows

From Anglo-Saxon agreements, till death do us part.

Posted September 13, 2026

Key points
  • Wedding vows started as secular oaths and have shifted over time.
  • The familiar wording heard at many modern weddings came from medieval religious rites.
  • Writing one’s own vows echoes early Anglo-Saxon rituals.

Anyone who has ever attended a typical wedding is likely acquainted with traditions like the walk down the aisle, the exchange of vows and the kiss to seal the deal, but why are wedding vows such an important part of marriage ceremonies and where did they come from in the first place?

Ancient Marriage

Marriage itself dates back millennia, traced as far back as 2350 BCE in Mesopotamia, or what is modern day Iraq. Early marriages, though, were less about love and more about carrying on bloodlines or making advantageous alliances.

Early documents detailing what should be included in marriage pledges have been found written in Old English, the precursor to today’s language that held sway in England between about 450 and 1100 A.D. This suggests that something somewhat like betrothal vows were part of marriage practices in Anglo-Saxon culture.

But such marriage pledges typically were agreements negotiated by a suitor and a woman’s male relatives. They echoed the form of, and were probably based on, oaths of service, protection, and faithfulness sworn between lords and vassals. In them, a suitor pledged to protect and take care of his wife and, if she accepted the betrothal, she pledged to serve him and follow his will.

No Wedding Banquets…Yet

Since such agreements were publicly witnessed, they were difficult to break. Though they might have been blessed or sometimes witnessed by clergy, marriage was in the Anglo-Saxon era not a religious practice, nor do we find much evidence of actual wedding events per se.

After some sort of agreement was negotiated, a celebratory gathering might have occurred at some point, particularly among wealthier families. However, specific wedding vows or rituals do not appear to have been required and, among poorer families, informal unions without agreements or fanfare were probably common.

This does not mean that there were no vows said between those slated to become husband and wife, but no written evidence of English vows predating the Norman Conquest in 1066 has been found.

The Making of a Vow

Wedding ceremony in a church
Source: Joshua Choate/Pixabay

The familiar “To have and to hold, for better or for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health” phrasing heard today at Christian weddings did not become formalized until 1549, when a priest in the Anglican church by the name of Thomas Cranmer recorded them in the Book of Common Prayer, appearing very close to how they are said still today.

But Cranmer was not the inventor of the vows. Instead, he adapted them from a larger medieval liturgical tradition known as the Sarum rites. The Sarum rites were associated with the Salisbury Cathedral in southern England and became the most influential public worship practices between the 12th and 16th centuries in England.

The specific marriage service Cranmer included in the Book of Common Prayer originated around the 12th century, as ecclesiastical blessing became a more integral part of the marriage event. Some scholars believe the wording arose from vows that had been recited by couples prior to the Norman Invasion but were at that point only part of oral traditions.

One small change put into place in the 1600s was that “Until death us depart” became the now more familiar “Till death us do part.” This change was made because the word “depart,” which originally meant something along the lines of “sever” or “separate,” had shifted toward a newer, and less apt, sense of “to leave” or “go away.”

Personalizing the Wedding Vow

A look back at the history of marriage shows that vows have taken varied forms over time.

Whether a couple repeats the centuries-old formula or makes new promises of their own, wedding vows serve the same basic purpose they have long held: to publicly mark the bond and permanence of marriage and to affirm that the union is one the couple has willingly entered.

Writing one’s own vows might seem thoroughly modern, but it’s not that far a cry from the oaths made long ago in Anglo-Saxon times. Even the kiss that seals the deal hearkens back to the kiss on the lips required to seal alliances when making oaths in feudal days.

So, it turns out, that the requisite “something old” featured in today’s modern wedding ceremonies is already simply part of the vows themselves.
